query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, controlled thermal aging promotes the preferential growth of stable intermetallic compounds from a metastable, finely dispersed solid-solution matrix. This phase evolution alters local electrochemical potentials and oxide‐scale formation kinetics, which in turn shifts the corrosion potential and modifies high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) exhibiting a metastable microstructure composed of a solid-solution matrix interspersed with embryonic intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermal aging protocol designed to stimulate intermetallic growth without exceeding the density and processing constraints.
generation.conditions: Reproducible, well-defined temperature/time profiles for thermal aging compared to an identical as-cast baseline alloy; testing performed under corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized growth and coarsening of intermetallic compounds driven by differential Mg diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging accelerates the diffusion of Mg relative to other constituents, leading to enhanced nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic phases. These evolved phases modify the local electrochemical landscape and promote changes in the kinetics and adhesion of protective oxide scales, thereby influencing corrosion and oxidation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the metastable as-cast baseline, the thermally aged alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable shift in corrosion potential (toward a more noble value or a distinct shift) and altered high-temperature oxidation kinetics (e.g., differences in oxide scale growth rate or adherence).
generation.baseline: As-cast, non-equilibrium microstructure of the alloy before any thermal aging treatment.
generation.boundary: Alloy composition and processing must preserve the density below 6 g/cm³; thermal aging should remain within temperature/time regimes that promote intermetallic evolution without inducing excessive grain growth or other dominant microstructural transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the shifts in corrosion potential and oxidation kinetics is uncertain due to potential variations in intermetallic phase distribution and local compositional inhomogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples (all meeting the density constraint). One set is retained in the as-cast condition, while the other is subjected to the controlled thermal aging protocol. Both sets are then exposed to identical corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion potential and current density) to assess shifts in corrosion behavior.
Thermogravimetric analysis and oxide scale characterization (e.g., via SEM/EDS) to compare oxidation kinetics and oxide layer properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show statistically significant differences in corrosion potentials and oxidation kinetics (i.e., oxide scale formation and adherence) relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis—asserting that intermetallic evolution drives these changes—is falsified.

Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. frame.understanding: Hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the as-cast microstructure features a finely dispersed metastable solid-solution matrix interspersed with embryonic intermetallic precipitates. Under service-simulated aging conditions, differential diffusion rates of Mg relative to the other constituents drive the localized growth of intermetallic compounds. This phase transformation alters the local electrochemical potential and modifies the formation kinetics and adhesion of the protective oxide scales. In a controlled comparison, an alloy maintained in the metastable state (baseline) should display distinct corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to an equivalent alloy thermally treated to promote the evolution of stable intermetallic phases. Predictions include (a) a measurable shift in corrosion potential and (b) altered oxidation kinetics that are directly correlated with the degree of intermetallic evolution. Boundary conditions require that the alloy compositions adhere strictly to the density constraint (<6 g/cm³) and that thermal aging is performed under reproducible, well-defined temperature/time profiles. Supporting prior observations include reports that Mg content influences phase stability and that compositionally graded architectures yield region-specific performance. The hypothesis would be falsified if controlled thermal treatment promoting phase evolution does not result in predictable corrosion or oxidation behavior changes relative to the metastable baseline, suggesting that factors other than intermetallic evolution control surface reactivity.
